column2: singleMsg builds one message with quotes and newlines. The title/summary deliberately include `"` and `\n`:
these are precisely the inputs most likely to produce invalid JSON through template interpolation.
batchMsg builds a batch summary message.
capturePost starts a fake receiver and returns request bodies and headers to the assertion function.
TestDingTalkBusinessErrorIsPermanent locks down HTTP 200 with nonzero errcode.
Ignoring errcode records failed delivery as success, a pitfall shared by domestic IM platforms.
Build a Chinese batch summary long enough to exceed 4096 bytes.
A configured secret requires signing parameters, or Feishu rejects it with 19021.
Card elements should include a button whose url points to vulnerability details.
Titles and summaries come from targets/model output and are untrusted.
This is why the default template exists: quotes and newlines in titles make naive
`"title": "{{.Title}}"` interpolation invalid JSON; {{json .}} avoids that.
Numbers must be JSON numbers, not strings (json:"...,string" would cause this pitfall).
Chinese subjects require RFC 2047 encoding to avoid garbled client display.
The body is base64; decoding should yield valid HTML.
The original title appears in text content: double quotes are valid HTML text and need no escaping.
Assert verbatim preservation to prevent unnecessary quote escaping that would display Chinese quotes
as ".
TestEmailEscapesStructuralInjection covers the injections email bodies actually need to prevent:
vulnerability titles and summaries are untrusted target/model output. Text positions must escape
& < > to prevent injected tags; attribute positions must also escape quotes to prevent closing href.
Backlinks use administrator-configured public_base_url and are relatively trusted, but attributes must still
escape quotes, or a quoted URL could close href and inject an event handler.
Validation errors are shown directly to configurators; identify missing fields rather than merely saying configuration is invalid.
TestEmailSMTPErrorClassification locks down SMTP 4xx/5xx semantics.
Treating 4xx as permanent would make a greylisting server move each notification to failed on its first
attempt, precisely where automatic retries should help.
If no reply code is available, classify as retryable: prefer an extra attempt over permanently rejecting a potentially transient
failure.
Whatever the classification, preserve original text for troubleshooting.
All six channels are required; missing one silently removes it from the UI dropdown.
This file adds email protocol tests. Previously email.Send coverage was zero:
no test exercised SMTP, despite its having the largest protocol surface of the six channels
and many failure modes (handshake, authentication, envelope, and DATA have distinct semantics).
Use a minimal real SMTP server rather than mocking net/smtp:
most email-channel risk lies in communicating with an actual SMTP server;
mocking that interaction would leave it untested.
fakeSMTP is a minimal SMTP server supporting greet/EHLO/AUTH/MAIL/RCPT/DATA/QUIT
and configurable reply codes for particular stages.
rcptReply is the RCPT TO reply, defaulting to 250.
mailReply is the MAIL FROM reply, defaulting to 250.
advertiseAuth advertises AUTH PLAIN in EHLO when true.
Do not advertise STARTTLS: exercise plaintext (the envelope logic is under test, not TLS).
Simplification: accept the PLAIN initial response directly, even if it spans lines.
The envelope must reach sender, two recipients, and DATA.
The body is base64 HTML and must contain actual vulnerability content, still recognizable after encoding.
All recipients must appear in the To header.
Do not send AUTH without a configured account; some relays reject it.
TestEmailSendClassifiesSMTPReplies directly verifies the audit fix:
5xx is permanent; 4xx (greylisting) is retryable.
Preserve server text so users know whether to contact the administrator or correct the address.
net/smtp PlainAuth refuses credentials on unencrypted connections unless the destination is localhost.
This is **correct** security behavior and must not be bypassed; provide an actionable error.
Use a non-localhost hostname to trigger it.
Not localhost.
Either connection failure or refusal to send credentials passes; the key is **never** silently transmitting the password.
Email has the most configuration fields; omissions otherwise surface only at delivery. Check each
is rejected early. Assertions require errors to identify the missing field.
TestEmailConfigTolerance covers configuration decoding tolerance: JSONB numbers are float64,
but users may enter ports as strings in the UI; arrays may also be a single string.
Port as a string.
Single string rather than an array.
Boolean as a string.
TestFilterValidateRejectsTypo directly verifies the audit fix:
reject threshold typos at write time, or filtering silently degrades to pushing everything.
Realistic typos; all must be rejected.
Errors should guide users toward a correction.
TestFilterValidateIsWriteTimeOnly locks down strict writes and tolerant reads:
existing invalid database values must not prevent channel loading, suddenly stopping historical channels.
No error.
The channel can still evaluate events without panic or blocking.
Malformed JSON, empty input, and incorrectly typed fields must all fall back to a zero-value Filter,
meaning no filtering. This enforces the preference for extra notifications over missed ones:
returning errors or partial parses here could silently discard all critical notifications after a one-character typo.
A zero-value Filter must match any event.
Unknown severity ranks as 0 and should be blocked by any nonempty threshold (do not send when uncertain).
Exclusion wins over inclusion: matching both must reject the event.
Ignore whitespace-only keywords, or matching degenerates to all strings containing spaces.
Disabled by default: vulnerability notifications usually mean new discoveries, not status-transition logs.
Creation events are unaffected by on_status_change.
This file covers doJSON HTTP-layer error classification.
Why test separately: channel adapters handle platform business codes (DingTalk errcode,
Feishu code, Telegram ok), while doJSON centrally classifies the **HTTP layer**;
these are independent defenses. Without this one, a gateway 503 could be permanent,
abandoning retries, while a 403 could waste three backoff rounds.
Errors must include the status code so users can distinguish configuration mistakes from peer failure.
Assert numeric codes, not Go's English StatusText: the original package wording was Chinese
like the rest of the project; numeric codes provide stable, language-independent assertions.
TestDoJSONIncludesResponseSnippet covers snippet: include the peer's error explanation,
or users know only that delivery failed, not why it was refused.
TestDoJSONSnippetIsSingleLineAndBounded constrains snippet shape:
peer responses flow directly into last_error and frontend tables; multiline or oversized text breaks layout and payload bounds.
Response with newlines, tabs, and 5000 characters of oversized content.
A 200-character snippet plus fixed prefix must remain far smaller than the original response.
TestDoJSONRejectsOversizedResponse confirms bounded reads: an oversized peer response
must not be read entirely into memory (each delivery-history record stores last_error).
Keep the final 6 characters so users can recognize the bot.
For short credentials, exposing the final 6 characters would expose the whole credential.
Preserve noncredential fields unchanged so the UI can display them.
For unrecognized channels, prefer empty configuration over exposing raw content that may contain credentials.
Masking is presentation-only; it must never alter the real stored value.
The user changed only method; the browser submits the masked value plus the new method.
Preserve omitted fields (partial-update semantics).
TestPrepareConfigUpdateBlocksDestinationSwap enforces the package's most important security invariant:
**changing the destination must not carry old credentials along**.
These cases use actual attack-shaped inputs (destination-only edits omitting credentials),
not valid defensive inputs; testing only the latter could pass even with ineffective protection.
wantMissing lists credential keys expected to be named in the error.
Masked values mean reusing old credentials, which must also be rejected when the destination changes.
The error must tell the operator how to fix the problem.
TestPrepareConfigUpdateAllowsLegitimateEdits is the inverse: do not falsely block normal edits,
or users may bypass or remove the guard as too annoying.
TestPrepareConfigUpdatePortTypeTolerance covers an easy false positive:
frontend ports are JSON numbers (float64), as are values read from storage,
but actual value types may differ (int vs float64). Direct == could classify an unchanged value as changed,
prompting password re-entry after only a name edit; false alarms undermine trust in the protection.
Submit the same port as int.
Actually changing the port must be blocked.
TestPrepareConfigUpdateSurvivesRepeatedSaveWithBlankDestination covers optional
destination fields: blank Telegram base_url uses the official API.
Previously the second save permanently broke saving:
Creation stores base_url:"" (creation stores frontend config directly, bypassing MergeConfig).
-> First save: MergeConfig treats the empty string as explicit clearing and deletes the key.
-> Second save: incoming remains "", stored lacks the key; incorrectly classified as a destination change.
-> bot_token is masked -> 400 requiring credentials to be re-entered with the changed destination.
The user changed nothing but cannot save again without repasting the Bot Token.
Frontend buildConfig() submits a value for each defined channel field: credentials use masked values,
empty text boxes use empty strings. Reproduce its full output, not just changed keys.
First save: only the channel name changed; config is returned unchanged.
Second save: identical submission; the user changed nothing.
Third save confirms saving remains consistently successful, not merely a one-time exception.
Credentials must remain throughout, unaffected by empty-string clearing.
TestPrepareConfigUpdateStillGuardsBlankDestinationChanges pairs with the previous
assertion: equating empty strings with missing keys **must not** permit actual destination changes.
Both directions can expose credentials: Telegram Bot Token is in the URL path,
so changing base_url sends the Token to the new address.
Direction one: blank (official URL) to a self-hosted address.
Direction two: clearing a self-hosted address (returning to the official API) also changes the destination.
Like SecretKeys, omitting destination-key declarations leaves a channel outside PrepareConfigUpdate's protection.
The compiler requires every channel to implement SecretKeys; additionally ensure no channel
returns an empty slice, which would expose its credentials in plaintext to the browser.
TestPrepareConfigUpdateRejectsMaskedInContainer covers an audit finding:
when a masked sentinel is embedded in a **nonstring** structure (such as webhook.headers),
MergeConfig recognizes only prefixed strings as masked, so literal "__masked__" would be
stored as a real header value, silently breaking authentication without an error.
Masked sentinel embedded in an object.
Submitting the whole object with actual new values is still accepted.
